cards.q: What is the functional group of a carboxylic acid?
cards.a: The carboxyl group, \(\mathrm{-COOH}\): a \(\mathrm{C=O}\) and an \(\mathrm{O-H}\) on the same carbon.

answerFigure.alt: Displayed formula of ethanoic acid: a CH3 group bonded to a carbon that carries a double-bonded O and an O–H group.

cards.why: Write it as \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) (or \(\mathrm{-CO_{2}H}\)), not \(\mathrm{-COHO}\).

cards.q: Name this carboxylic acid.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a four-carbon chain ending in a COOH group.

cards.a: Butanoic acid
cards.why: The carboxyl carbon is carbon 1 and is counted in the chain.

cards.q: Name this branched carboxylic acid.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a three-carbon chain ending in COOH, with a methyl branch on the carbon next to the COOH.

cards.a: 2-methylpropanoic acid
cards.why: It is an isomer of butanoic acid: same formula, branched chain.

cards.q: Name this compound, found in sorrel and many leafy vegetables.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a two-carbon molecule with a COOH group on each carbon.

cards.a: Ethanedioic acid (oxalic acid)
cards.why: Two carboxyl groups: the suffix becomes -dioic acid.

cards.q: Explain why ethanoic acid has a higher boiling temperature than propan-1-ol, although their relative molecular masses are the same (60).

figure.alt: Two ethanoic acid molecules facing each other, joined by two hydrogen bonds (dashed): the O–H hydrogen of each molecule bonds to the C=O oxygen of the other, forming a ring-shaped dimer.

cards.a: Ethanoic acid molecules form more hydrogen bonds, and pair up as dimers.
marks: Both have intermolecular hydrogen bonds through their \(\mathrm{O-H}\) groups.
In ethanoic acid, the \(\mathrm{C=O}\) oxygen can also accept a hydrogen bond, so there are more hydrogen bonds between molecules.
Pairs of acid molecules hydrogen bond together into dimers, effectively doubling the size of the particle.
More energy is needed to separate the molecules, so the boiling temperature is higher.

cards.q: Why are the first four carboxylic acids soluble in water, while hexadecanoic acid (palmitic acid, from palm oil) is not?
cards.a: The \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) group hydrogen bonds with water. In hexadecanoic acid the long non-polar hydrocarbon chain dominates and cannot hydrogen bond to water.
cards.why: Solubility falls as the hydrocarbon chain gets longer.

cards.q: Write an equation to show that ethanoic acid is a weak acid in water.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH(aq) \rightleftharpoons CH_{3}COO^{-}(aq) + H^{+}(aq)}\)
cards.why: It is only partially dissociated: the equilibrium lies well to the left.

cards.q: Write an equation for the reaction of ethanoic acid with sodium carbonate, and state what is seen.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{2CH_{3}COOH + Na_{2}CO_{3} \rightarrow 2CH_{3}COONa + CO_{2} + H_{2}O}\)
Effervescence (fizzing).
cards.why: Carboxylic acids are weak but strong enough to liberate \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) from carbonates; this is the test for a \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) group.

cards.q: Write an equation for the reaction of propanoic acid with sodium hydroxide, and name the organic product.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}COOH + NaOH \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}COONa + H_{2}O}\)
Sodium propanoate.

answerFigure.alt: Reaction scheme: propanoic acid reacts with sodium hydroxide solution to give sodium propanoate and water.

cards.why: An acid–base neutralisation: the carboxylic acid forms a carboxylate salt.

cards.q: How could you distinguish ethanoic acid from ethanol using sodium hydrogencarbonate solution?
cards.a: Ethanoic acid fizzes, giving \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) (which turns limewater milky). Ethanol does not react.
cards.why: Alcohols are far too weakly acidic to react with carbonates or hydrogencarbonates.

cards.q: How is a carboxylic acid made from a primary alcohol?
cards.a: Heat under reflux with excess acidified potassium dichromate(VI).

answerFigure.alt: Reaction scheme: ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid by excess acidified potassium dichromate(VI) under reflux.

cards.why: Reflux stops the intermediate aldehyde escaping, so it is oxidised further to the acid.

cards.q: Write an equation for the hydrolysis of propanenitrile by heating under reflux with dilute hydrochloric acid.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CN + 2H_{2}O + HCl \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}COOH + NH_{4}Cl}\)

answerFigure.alt: Reaction scheme: propanenitrile is hydrolysed to propanoic acid by heating under reflux with water and dilute hydrochloric acid; the nitrogen becomes ammonium chloride.

cards.why: The nitrogen ends up as ammonium ions; the \(\mathrm{-CN}\) carbon becomes the \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) carbon.

cards.q: Suggest a two-step route from bromoethane to propanoic acid.
cards.a:
1. Heat under reflux with KCN in ethanol: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}Br \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}CN}\).
2. Heat under reflux with dilute HCl: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CN \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}COOH}\).
cards.why: Forming the nitrile adds one carbon to the chain.

cards.q: Write an equation, using [H], for the reduction of ethanoic acid by \(\mathrm{LiAlH_{4}}\) in dry ether.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH + 4[H] \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}OH + H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: A carboxylic acid is reduced to a primary alcohol. \(\mathrm{NaBH_{4}}\) is not strong enough to do this.

cards.q: Write an equation for the reaction of ethanoic acid with phosphorus(V) chloride, and state what is seen.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH + PCl_{5} \rightarrow CH_{3}COCl + POCl_{3} + HCl}\)
Steamy (misty) fumes of HCl.

answerFigure.alt: Reaction scheme: ethanoic acid is converted to ethanoyl chloride by phosphorus(V) chloride at room temperature; POCl3 and HCl are also formed.

cards.why: The \(\mathrm{-OH}\) is replaced by \(\mathrm{-Cl}\), giving an acyl chloride.

cards.q: What are the conditions for making an ester from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol?
cards.a: Heat the acid and alcohol with a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid as a catalyst.
cards.why: The reaction is reversible and slow, so it does not go to completion.

cards.q: Write an equation for the reaction of ethanoic acid with ethanol, and name the ester.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH + CH_{3}CH_{2}OH \rightleftharpoons CH_{3}COOCH_{2}CH_{3} + H_{2}O}\)
Ethyl ethanoate.

answerFigure.alt: Reaction scheme: ethanoic acid and ethanol give ethyl ethanoate and water, with concentrated sulfuric acid as catalyst.

cards.why: The alcohol part is named first (ethyl), then the acid part (ethanoate).

cards.q: What is the functional group of an ester?
cards.a: \(\mathrm{-COO-}\): a carbon with a \(\mathrm{C=O}\), also single-bonded to an oxygen that joins a second carbon chain.

answerFigure.alt: Displayed formula of the ester group in methyl ethanoate: CH3 bonded to a carbon carrying a double-bonded O and a single-bonded O, which is bonded to a second CH3.

cards.why: The general formula is \(\mathrm{RCOOR'}\).

cards.q: Name this ester.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of an ester: a three-carbon acid part (with the C=O) joined through an oxygen to a one-carbon group.

cards.a: Methyl propanoate
cards.why: The carbon chain on the single-bonded O (one carbon, methyl) comes first; the chain containing C=O (three carbons, propanoate) second.

cards.q: Give the name of this ester.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of an ester: a two-carbon acid part (with the C=O) joined through an oxygen to a three-carbon chain.

cards.a: Propyl ethanoate
cards.why: Propyl from the alcohol (propan-1-ol); ethanoate from the acid (ethanoic acid).

cards.q: Name this ester, and name the acid and alcohol it is made from.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of an ester: an H–C=O group joined through an oxygen to a two-carbon chain.

cards.a: Ethyl methanoate, made from methanoic acid and ethanol.
cards.why: It is an isomer of methyl ethanoate and of propanoic acid, all \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{6}O_{2}}\).

cards.q: Draw the skeletal formula of ethyl butanoate, which gives pineapple its flavour.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}COOCH_{2}CH_{3}}\)

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of ethyl butanoate: a four-carbon chain with C=O at the end, joined through an oxygen to a two-carbon chain.

cards.why: The butanoate part contains the C=O; the ethyl group is on the single-bonded oxygen.

cards.q: Give four common uses of esters.
cards.a: Solvents (ethyl ethanoate in nail-varnish remover and glues), plasticisers, perfumes, and food flavourings.
cards.why: Many esters are volatile and have pleasant, fruity smells.

cards.q: Why are esters used as plasticisers, and what do plasticisers do?
cards.a: Plasticiser molecules fit between polymer chains (for example in PVC), pushing them apart so they slide past each other and the plastic becomes flexible.
cards.why: Large, involatile esters are used, so they stay in the plastic.

cards.q: Write an equation for the acid hydrolysis of methyl propanoate.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}COOCH_{3} + H_{2}O \rightleftharpoons CH_{3}CH_{2}COOH + CH_{3}OH}\)

answerFigure.alt: Reaction scheme: methyl propanoate and water give propanoic acid and methanol, heated under reflux with dilute acid.

cards.why: Acid hydrolysis is the reverse of esterification, so it is reversible.

cards.q: Write an equation for the hydrolysis of methyl propanoate by sodium hydroxide solution.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}COOCH_{3} + NaOH \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}COONa + CH_{3}OH}\)

answerFigure.alt: Reaction scheme: methyl propanoate heated under reflux with sodium hydroxide solution gives sodium propanoate and methanol.

cards.why: Alkaline hydrolysis gives the salt of the acid, not the acid itself.

cards.q: Explain why alkaline hydrolysis of an ester goes to completion, whereas acid hydrolysis does not.
cards.a: The carboxylate ion formed in alkali cannot react with the alcohol, so the reaction cannot reverse.
marks: Acid hydrolysis is the reverse of esterification, so an equilibrium mixture forms.
In alkali, the acid formed is converted to its carboxylate ion, \(\mathrm{RCOO^{-}}\).
The carboxylate ion does not react with the alcohol to re-form the ester, so the reaction is not reversible.
All the ester can therefore be hydrolysed.

cards.q: After an ester is hydrolysed with sodium hydroxide, how is the free carboxylic acid obtained?
cards.a: Add a strong acid such as dilute hydrochloric acid, which protonates the carboxylate ion.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{RCOO^{-} + H^{+} \rightarrow RCOOH}\): many acids, such as benzoic acid, then crystallise out.

cards.q: What are vegetable oils and animal fats, chemically?
cards.a: Esters of propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol) with long-chain carboxylic acids (fatty acids): each glycerol is joined to three acid chains (a triglyceride).

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol): a three-carbon chain with an OH group on each carbon.

cards.why: Palm oil, shea butter and groundnut oil are all mixtures of triglycerides.

cards.q: Glyceryl tributanoate (tributyrin) is a fat found in butter. Which acid and which alcohol are formed when it is hydrolysed?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of glyceryl tributanoate: a three-carbon glycerol backbone, each carbon joined through an ester linkage to a four-carbon butanoate chain.

cards.a: Butanoic acid (or its salt) and propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol).
cards.why: Three ester links break, giving three butanoate units and one glycerol.

cards.q: What is soap, and how is it made?
cards.a: Soap is the sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids. It is made by heating a vegetable oil or animal fat with sodium (or potassium) hydroxide, which also gives glycerol.
cards.why: This alkaline hydrolysis of fats is called saponification.

cards.q: African black soap is traditionally made by boiling palm kernel oil or shea butter with water filtered through the ash of burnt plantain skins and cocoa pods. Explain the chemistry.
cards.a: The ash makes an alkaline solution that hydrolyses the fats into soap and glycerol.
marks: The ash contains potassium compounds (such as potassium carbonate and hydroxide), so the solution is alkaline.
The oils and fats are esters (triglycerides) of glycerol.
Heating with alkali hydrolyses the ester links.
The products are potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids (soap) and propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol).

cards.q: Write an equation for the alkaline hydrolysis of glyceryl tributanoate by sodium hydroxide.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{5}(OOCC_{3}H_{7})_{3} + 3NaOH \rightarrow C_{3}H_{5}(OH)_{3} + 3C_{3}H_{7}COONa}\)
cards.why: One mole of fat needs three moles of hydroxide, one for each ester link.

cards.q: What is biodiesel, and how is it made?
cards.a: A mixture of methyl esters of long-chain carboxylic acids, made by reacting vegetable oils with methanol in the presence of a catalyst (such as KOH).
cards.why: Glycerol is the by-product.

cards.q: Write an equation for making biodiesel from a triglyceride \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{5}(OOCR)_{3}}\) and methanol.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{5}(OOCR)_{3} + 3CH_{3}OH \rightarrow 3RCOOCH_{3} + C_{3}H_{5}(OH)_{3}}\)
cards.why: Each ester link swaps its glycerol part for a methyl group: three methyl esters form.

cards.q: Jatropha, which grows on poor land in countries such as Mali and Ghana, has seeds rich in oil. Suggest why it has been promoted as a source of biodiesel.
cards.a: Its oil can be converted to biodiesel with methanol, giving a renewable fuel without using food crops or good farmland.
cards.why: Biodiesel is renewable, and the plants absorb carbon dioxide as they grow.

cards.q: What is the functional group of an acyl chloride? Name this one.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a two-carbon molecule with a C=O group and a Cl atom on the same carbon.

cards.a: \(\mathrm{-COCl}\). This is ethanoyl chloride, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCl}\).
cards.why: Name acyl chlorides from the acid: ethanoic acid → ethanoyl chloride.

cards.q: Name this compound.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a benzene ring carrying a COCl group.

cards.a: Benzoyl chloride
cards.why: It is the acyl chloride of benzoic acid.

cards.q: Name this compound and describe its structure.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of two CH3–C=O groups joined to the same oxygen atom.

cards.a: Ethanoic anhydride, \(\mathrm{(CH_{3}CO)_{2}O}\): two acyl groups joined through one oxygen atom.
cards.why: It is formally two ethanoic acid molecules joined with the loss of water.

cards.q: Name these two amides.

figure.alt: Skeletal formulae of two amides side by side: on the left, CH3–C(=O)–NH2; on the right, CH3–C(=O)–NH–CH3.

cards.a: Ethanamide, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CONH_{2}}\), and N-methylethanamide, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CONHCH_{3}}\).
cards.why: N- shows the methyl group is on the nitrogen. These are made from ethanoyl chloride with ammonia and with methylamine.

cards.q: What type of reaction do acyl chlorides and acid anhydrides undergo with water, alcohols, ammonia and amines?
cards.a: Nucleophilic addition–elimination.
cards.why: The nucleophile adds to the δ+ carbonyl carbon, then the C=O re-forms and a small molecule (HCl, or a carboxylic acid from an anhydride) is eliminated.

cards.q: Write an equation for the reaction of ethanoyl chloride with water, and state what is seen.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCl + H_{2}O \rightarrow CH_{3}COOH + HCl}\)
A vigorous reaction giving steamy fumes of HCl.

answerFigure.alt: Reaction scheme: ethanoyl chloride and water give ethanoic acid and hydrogen chloride at room temperature.

cards.why: Acyl chlorides are hydrolysed much faster than chloroalkanes.

cards.q: Write an equation for the reaction of ethanoyl chloride with ethanol.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCl + CH_{3}CH_{2}OH \rightarrow CH_{3}COOCH_{2}CH_{3} + HCl}\)

answerFigure.alt: Reaction scheme: ethanoyl chloride and ethanol give ethyl ethanoate and hydrogen chloride at room temperature.

cards.why: Unlike esterification with the acid, this is fast and goes to completion.

cards.q: Write an equation for the reaction of ethanoyl chloride with concentrated ammonia.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCl + 2NH_{3} \rightarrow CH_{3}CONH_{2} + NH_{4}Cl}\)

answerFigure.alt: Reaction scheme: ethanoyl chloride and ammonia give ethanamide and hydrogen chloride; with excess ammonia the HCl forms ammonium chloride.

cards.why: The HCl formed reacts with a second \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) to give ammonium chloride.

cards.q: Write an equation for the reaction of ethanoyl chloride with methylamine, and name the organic product.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCl + 2CH_{3}NH_{2} \rightarrow CH_{3}CONHCH_{3} + CH_{3}NH_{3}^{+}Cl^{-}}\)
N-methylethanamide.

answerFigure.alt: Reaction scheme: ethanoyl chloride and methylamine give N-methylethanamide and hydrogen chloride; with excess amine the HCl forms methylammonium chloride.

cards.why: A primary amine gives an N-substituted amide; the second amine molecule removes the HCl.

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the reaction of ethanoyl chloride with water.
cards.a: Nucleophilic addition–elimination.

answerFigure.alt: Addition–elimination of water with ethanoyl chloride: a lone pair on the water oxygen attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon and C=O breaks; in the intermediate the C=O re-forms, chloride leaves, and an O–H bond breaks to lose H+, giving ethanoic acid and HCl.

marks: Lone pair on the O of \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon; arrow from \(\mathrm{C=O}\) to O.
Intermediate with \(\mathrm{O^{-}}\), and \(\mathrm{O^{+}}\) on the added water.
Arrow from the \(\mathrm{O^{-}}\) lone pair to re-form \(\mathrm{C=O}\), and arrow from the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond to Cl.
Arrow from an \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond to \(\mathrm{O^{+}}\) to show loss of \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\).

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the reaction of ethanoyl chloride with ethanol.
cards.a: Nucleophilic addition–elimination; the products are ethyl ethanoate and HCl.

answerFigure.alt: Addition–elimination of ethanol with ethanoyl chloride: the ethanol oxygen lone pair attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon and C=O breaks; the C=O re-forms, chloride leaves and the O–H bond breaks, giving ethyl ethanoate and HCl.

marks: Lone pair on the O of ethanol attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon; arrow from \(\mathrm{C=O}\) to O.
Tetrahedral intermediate with \(\mathrm{O^{-}}\) and \(\mathrm{O^{+}}\).
\(\mathrm{C=O}\) re-forms and \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) is eliminated.
\(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) is lost from the \(\mathrm{O^{+}}\) (arrow from O–H bond to O).

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the reaction of ethanoyl chloride with ammonia.
cards.a: Nucleophilic addition–elimination; ethanamide forms.

answerFigure.alt: Addition–elimination of ammonia with ethanoyl chloride: the nitrogen lone pair attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon and C=O breaks; in the intermediate the C=O re-forms, chloride leaves and an N–H bond breaks to lose H+, giving ethanamide.

marks: Lone pair on N of \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon.
Arrow from the \(\mathrm{C=O}\) bond to O, giving an intermediate with \(\mathrm{O^{-}}\) and \(\mathrm{N^{+}}\).
\(\mathrm{O^{-}}\) lone pair re-forms \(\mathrm{C=O}\); \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond breaks.
Arrow from an \(\mathrm{N-H}\) bond to \(\mathrm{N^{+}}\) (a second \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) removes the \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\)).

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the reaction of ethanoyl chloride with methylamine.
cards.a: Nucleophilic addition–elimination; N-methylethanamide forms.

answerFigure.alt: Addition–elimination of methylamine with ethanoyl chloride: the nitrogen lone pair attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon and C=O breaks; the C=O re-forms, chloride leaves and N–H breaks to lose H+, giving N-methylethanamide.

marks: Lone pair on N of \(\mathrm{CH_{3}NH_{2}}\) attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon; arrow from \(\mathrm{C=O}\) to O.
Intermediate with \(\mathrm{O^{-}}\) and \(\mathrm{N^{+}}\).
\(\mathrm{C=O}\) re-forms and \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) leaves.
Loss of \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) from \(\mathrm{N^{+}}\).

cards.q: Explain why the carbonyl carbon of an acyl chloride is so readily attacked by nucleophiles.
cards.a: Two electronegative atoms, O and Cl, pull electron density away from the carbon, making it strongly δ+.
marks: Oxygen and chlorine are both more electronegative than carbon.
The carbonyl carbon is therefore strongly δ+.
Nucleophiles (with a lone pair) are attracted to it, and \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) is a good leaving group.

cards.q: Write an equation for the reaction of ethanoic anhydride with methanol.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{(CH_{3}CO)_{2}O + CH_{3}OH \rightarrow CH_{3}COOCH_{3} + CH_{3}COOH}\)

answerFigure.alt: Reaction scheme: ethanoic anhydride and methanol give methyl ethanoate and ethanoic acid.

cards.why: An anhydride reacts like an acyl chloride, but eliminates a carboxylic acid instead of HCl.

cards.q: Write an equation for the reaction of ethanoic anhydride with ammonia.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{(CH_{3}CO)_{2}O + 2NH_{3} \rightarrow CH_{3}CONH_{2} + CH_{3}COONH_{4}}\)
cards.why: The ethanoic acid formed reacts with a second \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) to give ammonium ethanoate.

cards.q: Aspirin is made from 2-hydroxybenzoic acid and ethanoic anhydride. Write the equation.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{HOC_{6}H_{4}COOH + (CH_{3}CO)_{2}O \rightarrow CH_{3}COOC_{6}H_{4}COOH + CH_{3}COOH}\)

answerFigure.alt: Reaction scheme: 2-hydroxybenzoic acid is converted to aspirin by warming with ethanoic anhydride and a phosphoric acid catalyst; ethanoic acid is the by-product.

cards.why: The phenol \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group is acylated, forming an ester link.

cards.q: Give the industrial advantages of using ethanoic anhydride rather than ethanoyl chloride to make aspirin.
cards.a: Ethanoic anhydride is cheaper, safer and easier to control.
marks: It is cheaper.
It is less corrosive and reacts less violently, so the reaction is easier to control.
It does not react as readily with water (moisture in the air).
It does not produce toxic, corrosive HCl gas; the by-product is ethanoic acid.

cards.q: Describe how impure aspirin is purified by recrystallisation.
cards.a: Dissolve in the minimum hot solvent, filter hot if needed, cool to crystallise, then filter, wash and dry.
marks: Dissolve the impure solid in the minimum volume of hot solvent.
Filter the hot solution (if needed) to remove insoluble impurities.
Cool slowly so that pure crystals form; soluble impurities stay in solution.
Filter under reduced pressure, wash with a little cold solvent and leave to dry.

cards.q: How does the melting point show whether a sample of aspirin is pure?
cards.a: A pure solid melts sharply at the value in the data book. An impure solid melts lower and over a wider range.
cards.why: Measure it with a melting-point apparatus and compare it with the literature value.

cards.q: A crude sample of ethyl ethanoate contains ethanoic acid, ethanol and water. Outline how a pure, dry sample is obtained.
cards.a: Neutralise the acid, separate the layers, dry, then distil.
marks: Shake with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution in a separating funnel, releasing the pressure, to remove the acid.
Run off and discard the lower aqueous layer.
Dry the ester layer with an anhydrous drying agent such as anhydrous calcium chloride or magnesium sulfate.
Distil, collecting the fraction that boils at the boiling point of the ester.

cards.q: Why must the separating funnel be inverted and its tap opened regularly when ethyl ethanoate is shaken with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution?
cards.a: The acid reacts with the hydrogencarbonate to make \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\), and the pressure must be released.
cards.why: Otherwise the stopper can be forced out.

cards.q: True or false: hydrolysing an ester with sodium hydroxide gives the carboxylic acid and the alcohol.
cards.a: False. It gives the sodium salt of the acid and the alcohol.
cards.why: The free acid is only obtained after acidifying the mixture.

cards.q: True or false: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOCH_{2}CH_{3}}\) is called ethanoyl ethyl.
cards.a: False. It is ethyl ethanoate: the alkyl group from the alcohol comes first, then the acid part ending in -oate.
cards.why: Ethanoyl is the name of the CH3CO– group, used in acyl chlorides such as ethanoyl chloride.

cards.q: True or false: carboxylic acids are strong acids because they react with carbonates to release carbon dioxide.
cards.a: False. They are weak acids (only partly dissociated), but still strong enough to release carbon dioxide from carbonates.
cards.why: Carbonic acid is an even weaker acid, so carboxylic acids can displace it.
